## What you hand in, and when

There is **no final exam** in Course I and **no progress presentation**. The term project (40 % of the grade) consists of

| Part | Weight | Due |
|---|:---:|---|
| Proposal (`W08_project_proposal.ipynb`) | 5 % | before Week 9 — done |
| **Final report and code** | **25 %** | **one week after the Week 16 session** (you can use the feedback from your talk) |
| **Final presentation** (including live questions on your code) | **10 %** | in the Week 16 session; slides uploaded **before** the session |

The Week 16 session starts with the 10-minute quiz on the Week 15 lecture; the presentations follow.

**Submit** (one folder or zip, named `AMPS1_project_<student-ID>`):

1. `project.ipynb` — the Colab notebook that produces **every** number and figure in the report. It must run end to end after *Runtime → Restart session and run all*, with `%%fenicsx -np 2`.
2. `report.qmd` **and** the rendered `report.html` — start from `report_template/report.qmd`. Render it with `W16_render_report.ipynb` on Colab or with a local Quarto installation.
3. `figs/` — the figures used in the report, saved by `project.ipynb`.
4. The presentation slides (PDF or HTML).

## The report

At most **10 pages** in print (about 4 000 words plus figures), in English. Equations, tables and figures instead of prose wherever possible. The template contains every required section; keep the headings.

| Section | What must be in it |
|---|---|
| 1 Problem | Physical setting, governing equations, boundary and initial conditions, parameters **with units**, dimensionless numbers, the quantity of interest (QoI). Why it matters for your research. |
| 2 Weak form | Spaces, essential vs natural conditions, the residual $F(u;v)$, the Jacobian (derived, or `ufl.derivative` plus a check). Discretisation: elements, stabilisation, time stepping. |
| 3 Analysis | Which theorem gives existence/uniqueness/stability of the (linearised) problem — Lax–Milgram, inf-sup (Brezzi), monotonicity, a CFL or Péclet argument — and **where it can fail** for your parameters. |
| 4 Implementation | Structure of the code (one short table: function → purpose), solver choices (Newton/SNES options, linear solver, preconditioner) and **why** these. |
| 5 Verification | (a) MMS: the manufactured solution, the **predicted** rates, a convergence table/plot with **observed** rates on at least 4 meshes. (b) A benchmark, an analytical limit, or a conservation check, **with a citation**, and the deviation in %. (c) `-np 1` vs `-np 2` give the same QoI. |
| 6 Results | The QoI and a parameter study (e.g. in Re, Pe, a material parameter); mesh (and time-step) independence of the reported values. |
| 7 LLM workflow | What was generated by an LLM, which errors you found, **how** you found each one (which test failed), and how each component was verified. At least three concrete cases. |
| 8 Limitations | What your model and numerics cannot do; what you would do next. |
| References, AI-usage log | Cited sources (papers, textbooks, benchmark data). The AI-usage log table of the course, completed. |

**Numbers.** Every number in the report must come from a cell of `project.ipynb` that you ran. Put a short tag after each table or figure caption
naming the cell (e.g. *"project.ipynb §5.2"*). Do not round away disagreements: if the observed rate is 1.6 where you predicted 2, say so and explain.

## The code

- One notebook, ordered like the report (§2 forms → §5 verification → §6 results). Long runs save their results to `/tmp/fnx/*.npz` or to Google Drive; the plotting cells read them.
- `%%fenicsx -np 2` for every simulation; ordinary cells only NumPy and matplotlib (as in the weekly notebooks).
- Print the converged reason (KSP/SNES) of every solve that a reported number depends on.
- Total run time on Colab: **at most 30 minutes**. If the full study takes longer, run the expensive part once, save the results, and add a cell with a
  reduced version (coarser mesh) that reproduces the trend.
- Code you did not write (LLM, demos, tutorials) is allowed — and must be listed in the AI-usage log and the code-provenance note.

## The presentation

**12 minutes per student: 8 minutes talk + 4 minutes questions.** Strict timing.

1. Problem and QoI (1 slide)
2. Weak form and the one analysis point that matters for your problem (1–2 slides)
3. Verification: the MMS rate plot and the benchmark comparison (2 slides)
4. Results (1–2 slides)
5. One LLM error you found, and how (1 slide)

**Live questions on your code.** Have `project.ipynb` open. You will be asked to show where something happens in the code (e.g. where a boundary
condition enters, which line sets the Jacobian, what a solver option does) and to predict what a small change would do. Being unable to explain your
own submitted code counts as not having done that part (syllabus, *Academic Integrity*).

## Optional extension: a gradient-based inverse problem (bonus)

Projects with a model parameter (topics A–E of `projects/index.html`, or your own topic) may add an inverse problem: estimate the parameter $m$ from (synthetic) data by minimising
$J(m)=\tfrac12\int(u(m)-u_d)^2\,dx$ with a gradient computed by the **adjoint method**. Either with `dolfinx-adjoint` (installation cell in
`W16_render_report.ipynb`, tested with DOLFINx 0.11 on Colab), or by deriving and solving the adjoint equation yourself.

Required for the bonus — all three:

1. **Taylor test**: $|J(m+\epsilon\,\delta m)-J(m)-\epsilon\,dJ\cdot\delta m|=O(\epsilon^2)$, with the observed rate printed for at least 4 values of $\epsilon$.
2. The adjoint gradient agrees with a **central finite difference** (relative difference printed).
3. **Recovery**: data generated with a known $m_\text{true}$ (optionally with noise); the optimiser recovers $m_\text{true}$ (or explains the bias caused by the noise).

Put it in an extra report section "9 Inverse problem" (it does not count towards the 10 pages). Worth up to **+2 points** on the course grade; it never
lowers your score, and it cannot compensate a missing verification section. For **topic F** the inverse problem is the project itself; its bonus is the
design-optimisation stretch goal (F page, stretch goal 2), under the same three checks.
